analysis.one_liner: Requires every kind of health coverage to pay for HIV-prevention drugs with no out-of-pocket costs or prior approval.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 29 Senate Democrats as cosponsors in March 2026, the bill has sat in the Senate health committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require private health plans (including older plans that are normally exempt from the Affordable Care Act's preventive-care rules), Medicaid, CHIP, Medicare, the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program, VA care, and TRICARE to cover any FDA-approved drug for preventing HIV, plus the lab work, monitoring visits, and pharmacy fees that go with it, with no copays, deductibles, or coinsurance. Plans generally could not use prior authorization (getting the insurer's sign-off before a drug is dispensed) unless they cover a therapeutically equivalent PrEP drug freely. It would also make it illegal for life, disability, or long-term care insurers to deny or surcharge people just for taking HIV-prevention medication, fund public and provider education campaigns and grants for uninsured people, and guarantee confidentiality for people on a family member's plan.
analysis.who_benefits: People at risk of HIV — including Medicaid and CHIP enrollees, seniors on Medicare, veterans, service members and their families, and people with no insurance (through new grants) — who today face copays, deductibles, and insurer pre-approval hurdles for PrEP. Also PrEP users who have been denied or overcharged by life, disability, or long-term care insurers, and anyone on a family plan who fears the policyholder finding out they use the benefit.

how_it_helps.text: Requires private health plans — including grandfathered plans normally exempt from ACA preventive-coverage rules — to cover any FDA-approved HIV-prevention drug, its administrative fees, related lab work, and clinical follow-up with no cost-sharing [S2]
Bans prior-authorization requirements for those services unless a plan covers a therapeutically equivalent PrEP drug without prior authorization [S2]

Adds HIV prevention services as a mandatory Medicaid and CHIP benefit with no cost-sharing, including in benchmark and expansion plans, effective January 1, 2027, with a delay allowed for states that need to change their laws [S2]

Puts HIV prevention services under Medicare Part B with 100% payment and no Part B deductible, and requires Medicare Part D plans to waive the deductible and all cost-sharing for HIV-prevention drugs starting in 2027 [S2]

Eliminates VA medication copays and related charges for PrEP, requires TRICARE to cover HIV prevention treatment with no cost-sharing, and authorizes funding for the Indian Health Service to provide PrEP drugs, testing, and monitoring [S2]
Makes it unlawful for life, disability, or long-term care insurers to deny, limit, or raise premiums for anyone because they take HIV-prevention medication [S2]

Authorizes CDC public-education and provider-education campaigns targeted to communities where PrEP is underused, and a grant program for states, tribes, and nonprofits to serve uninsured and underinsured people [S2]

Requires federal regulators to change privacy rules so a person on a family plan can use these benefits without the policyholder being told, and gives people a private right of action, with attorney's fees, to sue over violations; insurers must submit annual compliance data for ten years [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Private insurers and the employers that sponsor health plans, through higher premiums for the no-cost-sharing coverage mandates; federal taxpayers, through Medicare, VA, TRICARE, Indian Health Service, and grant spending; and state budgets, through the new mandatory Medicaid and CHIP benefit. Life, disability, and long-term care insurers lose part of their pricing flexibility.

drawbacks.text: The public-education campaigns and the PrEP/PEP grant program are authorized at 'such sums as may be necessary' for fiscal years 2026–2030 — an open-ended funding commitment with no dollar cap [S2]

States that the HHS Secretary determines need new legislation to comply can delay the Medicaid and CHIP requirements until after their next legislative session, so the guarantee would not be immediate everywhere [S2]
The prior-authorization ban has an exception: a plan can still require pre-approval for a PrEP drug as long as it covers a therapeutically equivalent drug with no prior authorization [S2]

Adding a mandatory Medicaid and CHIP benefit with zero cost-sharing and eliminating Medicare cost-sharing creates new mandatory federal and state spending, and the private-coverage mandate is borne through premiums rather than appropriations [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health case is strong: PrEP is nearly 100% effective when taken as prescribed, and cost-sharing and prior authorization are the main documented barriers to the people most at risk. The costs — higher premiums and new Medicare, Medicaid, and state spending — are real but are spread across many payers, and preventing HIV infections avoids far more expensive lifelong treatment later. The bill's weakest points are its uncapped funding authorizations, the state-legislation delay loophole, and the carve-out that still permits prior authorization when an equivalent drug is freely covered.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in March 2026 and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote while Congress remains in session.

narrative.text: Senator Tina Smith introduced S. 3990 on March 4, 2026, with 19 senators originally joining; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day [S1] [S2] [S4]
It has since gained 29 Democratic cosponsors — all of them Democrats; no Republican has joined [S3]
The action history shows no further activity after the referral: no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action [S4]

The bill's text spells out mandatory no-cost-sharing coverage of HIV prevention services across private plans, Medicaid, CHIP, Medicare, FEHBP, VA, TRICARE, and the Indian Health Service, plus anti-discrimination rules for life, disability, and long-term care insurers [S2]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill has not moved, health insurers keep their current cost-sharing and prior-authorization practices for PrEP, and life and long-term care insurers keep their current underwriting rules; people at risk of HIV keep paying out of pocket or go without.

for.name: Sen. Tina Smith
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 19 original cosponsors

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by a Republican in this Congress)
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote since the bill was referred in March 2026

sides.party_line_note: All 29 cosponsors are Senate Democrats; not one of the 55 Senate Republicans has joined, and with Republicans holding the majority, the committee has taken no action.

industries.industry: Health insurers and employer health plans
industries.note: The bill forces them to cover PrEP drugs, labs, and follow-up with no cost-sharing and generally no prior authorization, extend that mandate to plans normally exempt from ACA preventive rules, and file annual compliance data for ten years. Insurers have used cost-sharing and pre-approval to keep PrEP uptake down; this bill removes those tools and passes the cost into premiums.

industries.industry: Life, disability, and long-term care insurers
industries.note: It becomes unlawful for these insurers to deny coverage, raise premiums, or condition coverage on whether an applicant takes HIV-prevention medication, removing a common underwriting ground. Enforcement is left to state insurance regulators.

Every payer in the bill — private plans, Medicaid, CHIP, Medicare Part B and D, VA, TRICARE, IHS, and the new grants — must pay for any FDA-approved HIV-prevention drug, including its administrative fees, guaranteeing a much larger insured market. The leading long-acting PrEP products are sold under patent at high prices, so the coverage guarantee flows revenue to those manufacturers even as it expands access.

industries.industry: Community health centers and HIV service nonprofits
industries.note: Federally qualified health centers, family planning grantees, rural clinics, and community-based organizations are directly eligible for new PrEP/PEP grant funding for drugs, outreach, and patient navigators, expanding their role in serving uninsured people.

analysis.trajectory: With Republicans holding 55 of 100 Senate seats, no Republican cosponsors, and no committee action since the March referral, the bill is unlikely to get a markup or floor vote; it will most likely die when this Congress ends in January 2027 unless it is attached to a larger, must-pass health package.
